case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital (CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal) c. D.P.
text:
Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish
General Hospital (CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal) c. D.P.

2024 QCCS 1990

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-129786-243

DATE:

May 29, 2024

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

MARK PHILLIPS, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

SIR MORTIMER B. DAVIS JEWISH GENERAL HOSPITAL,
a
health institution administered by

the CIUSSS DU
CENTRE-OUEST-DE-L’ÎLE-DE-MONTRÉAL

and

DR. LOUISE MINER

Plaintiffs

v.

D. P.

Defendant

and

S.
P.

Interested
person

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(
on application for authorization of care
)

_____________________________________________________________________

1.

BACKGROUND

[
1
]

The individual who is the subject of the present
application for authorization of care is a young man who has just reached the
age of majority
[1]
.

[
2
]

At the age of four, he was diagnosed with autism
spectrum disorder (ASD) and mild intellectual disability (ID).

[
3
]

Two-and-a-half years ago, when he was 16, he
experienced an initial episode of psychosis. This consisted of hallucinations
in the form of hearing voices, which can be very troubling for him.

[
4
]

While still a minor, D. received treatment on
the strength of substitute consent conferred by his mother
[2]
. Treatment was nevertheless ultimately abandoned, and D. suffered
episodes of aggression and other behaviours that put him and his family at
risk, as well as causing some damage to property.

[
5
]

Today, D. has been hospitalized for about the
last three months, voluntarily, at the Jewish General Hospital and is
undergoing treatment. The hospital is seeking a treatment order to three years
of antipsychotic and other medication. D.’s main bone of contention is with the
three-year duration, which he feels should be limited to half that period.

2.

ANALYSIS

2.1

Basic criteria

[
6
]

The evidence has established that the proposed
care is required for D.’s health. It has also established that it is a very
good plan, the benefits of which would likely outweigh the disadvantages.

[
7
]

It has also been established that D. has a
history of cessation of treatment, in particular when he experiences certain
side effects, notably in the form of restlessness (akathisia), which he finds
very irritating. It has been shown that in the absence of an order, he is
unlikely to persevere with pharmacological treatment.

[
8
]

All that is well and good. We must now turn to
the criterion of inability to consent, which must be satisfied, failing which
the Court is without jurisdiction to impose treatment against a person’s wishes.

2.2

Ability to consent

[
9
]

The hospital, and its two expert witnesses, a
psychiatrist and a resident in psychiatry, are of the view that D. is not
competent to refuse treatment. All three of his diagnoses are put forward as
contributing to his inability to consent.

[
10
]

As the central issue in the case, the hospital
pointed to the fact that side effects such as restlessness have, in the past,
caused D. to cease treatment, and that the same thing is therefore likely to
occur in the future in the absence of a Court order. The Court accepts those
two propositions as having been proven.

[
11
]

The difficulty lies in the fact that the
criterion that the Court is called upon to apply is not the utility or
necessity of a Court order for purposes of securing compliance with a treatment
plan whose potential merits have been duly demonstrated. In order to intervene
— which means violating the physical integrity of a human being by subjecting
him to medical treating against his will —, the Court must be satisfied that
the person is himself incapable of engaging in the rational process that
constitutes the weighing of pros and cons with a view to either giving or
withholding consent, according to certain criteria
[3]
.

[
12
]

In the present case, the hospital has not
discharged that burden.

[
13
]

Indeed, while the view was expressed that D.’s
three diagnoses prevent him from engaging meaningfully in that process, that opinion
took the form of a bald, unsupported assertion, with little or no detail. A
further witness stressed the allegedly superficial character of D.’s
understanding.

[
14
]

As required by law, the Court heard D.. Although
somewhat shy, he stated very clearly that he suffers from auditory
hallucinations, and that he wants them to stop. He understands that the
antipsychotic medication can help him. He has taken such medication in the past
and understands its benefits. He does not deny his disease. Quite the opposite.
He acknowledges it and even expressed his clear overarching objective of overcoming
it, in order to be “at peace.” He understands the nature of the proposed
treatment, and is prepared to agree to it, at least in the form of pills, but
not necessarily injections. He cannot be held to a standard of understanding
that would require mastery of the scientific intricacies of his disease. The
evidence also revealed that he has been researching the disease on the internet.
In sum, he is barely 18 years of age and is intellectually alert enough to be
curious to learn more about his disease.

[
15
]

In the view of the Court, the legal test for
inability to consent has not been met.

[
16
]

The application must therefore be dismissed.

2.3

Categorical refusal

[
17
]

As per a common understanding of certain jurisprudential
authority
[4]
, the parties also debated the criterion of categorical refusal.
However, that criterion does not apply in a case such as this.

[
18
]

Article 16 first paragraph C.C.Q. reads as
follows:

16.
L’autorisation du tribunal est nécessaire en cas d’empêchement ou de refus
injustifié de celui qui peut consentir à des soins requis par l’état de santé
d’un mineur ou d’un majeur inapte à donner son consentement; elle l’est
également si le majeur inapte à consentir refuse catégoriquement de recevoir
les soins, à moins qu’il ne s’agisse de soins d’hygiène ou d’un cas
d’urgence.

16. The authorization of
the court is necessary where the person who may give consent to care required
by the state of health of a minor or a person of full age who is incapable of
giving his consent is prevented from doing so or, without justification,
refuses to do so; it is also necessary where a person of full age who is
incapable of giving his consent categorically refuses to receive care, except
in the case of hygienic care or emergency.

[
19
]

As can be seen, this legislative provision sets out two distinct
scenarios in two propositions separated by a semicolon in both the English and
French text. When read in conjunction with articles 11 through 15, those
propositions mean the following.

2.3.1

Scenario I

[
20
]

Authorization for treatment from the Court is required: (a) where the
person is incapable of consenting himself and, (b) where substitute consent
cannot be secured, which can occur either: (i) where there is no person who has
been vested with legal authority to tender such consent, or (ii) where there is
such a person, but he or she has withheld consent unreasonably
[5]
.
That is the first scenario.

2.3.2

Scenario II

[
21
]

The second scenario is a situation where substitute consent has been
duly secured, but the person on whose behalf it was tendered not only refuses
the treatment, but does so “categorically,” i.e. vehemently and not merely
lukewarmly. In that case, the legislature has afforded the individual the
additional protection of requiring Court authorization.

2.3.3

Discussion

[
22
]

All that to say that in the first scenario, where the Court has
concluded that the person is himself incapable of giving or withholding
consent, and where substitute consent cannot be secured, the Court may
authorize the treatment if it is required and beneficial. There is no further
criterion of categorical refusal
[6]
.
If there were, that would mean that a person who is incapable of consenting and
who has no one to turn to who can consent for him, but whose refusal of
treatment is merely lukewarm and not categorical, would be in a legal vacuum,
the Court being powerless to intervene. That cannot have been the intent of the
legislature.

[
23
]

It is telling that the requirement of categorical
refusal is only raised in the second scenario, which is introduced by the words
“it is also necessary,” “it” being Court authorization. Likewise, the French
text reads: “
elle [l’autorisation du tribunal] l’est également
”, the pronoun “ l’ ” referring back to the word “
necessaire
.”
The requirement of categorical refusal is therefore clearly limited to the
second scenario.

[
24
]

It also flows from context that whereas the first scenario contemplates
some sort of snag in the working of the general principle of substitute consent
— which is clearly the general principle and which it is hoped will transpire
in the vast majority of real-life situations
[7]

— it follows that the second scenario must be dealing with the situation where,
despite substitute consent having been duly secured, the legislature has
nevertheless seen fit to protect the individual’s physical integrity from
unwanted intrusion by requiring that the matter be made subject to the scrutiny
of the Court.

[
25
]

In other words, normally, substitute consent that is
given puts an end to the matter and treatment is administered or not
accordingly. But where substitute consent is granted in favour of permitting
the treatment, and the person concerned puts up such resistance that can be
characterized as categorical refusal, then the matter must be referred to the
Court. No such consideration is in play where the person is helpless to consent
himself and also doubly helpless for lack of a person who can offer substitute
consent.

[
26
]

In this case, had the Court found D. to be incapable of
giving or withholding consent, the case would have fallen under scenario number
1, given that he has no tutor, mandatary or other person who can consent for
him. As just explained, in such a case, the institution seeking authorization
for treatment is not required to satisfy an additional criterion of categorical
refusal
[8]
.

[
27
]

Be that as it may, had the Court found that it needed
to turn its mind to the criterion of categorical refusal, it would have ruled
that D.’s agreement to treatment, triggered by the prospect of coming to
Court, remains limited to what are currently subtherapeutic doses of the
medication, and that his refusal can properly be characterized as categorical.

[
28
]

Needless to say, that conclusion does not change the
outcome.

3.

CONCLUSION

[
29
]

The Court is of the view that the professionals involved are highly
competent and clearly have D.’s best interests at heart. It is also of the view
that a Court order would perhaps be beneficial to D. in introducing an element
of coercion that would prevent future cessations of treatment in the future. It
is also true that without a Court order, D. is at greater risk than he would be
without the order.

[
30
]

The point, however, is that all of that remains insufficient. In order
to impose unwanted treatment, the Court must conclude that, on the balance of
probabilities, it has been shown that D. meets the criteria for the Court to
conclude that he is unable to consent. On the basis of the evidence presented,
the Court is forced to conclude that that burden of proof has not been
discharged here.

WHEREFORE, THE COURT:

[
31
]

DISMISSES
the
application, without costs.

reasonably
, that puts and end to the matter and the

obviously be a Court hearing to rule upon the reasonableness of the refusal put
forth by the person holding the power give or refuse consent on behalf of the
person who is incapable of doing so.
